Æfter þyssere sprǣċe cōmon ðā drȳmen, and hæfdon him mid tweġen ormǣte dracan, ðǣra orðung ācwealde þæt earme mennisċ: ac sē apostol Matheus þā dracan ġeswefode, and siððan of ðām lande adrǣfde, swā þæt hī næfre siððan þǣr ġesewene nǣron.

After this speech came the sorcerers, who had two enormous dragons which them, whose breath killed that poor man: but the apostle Matthew lulled the dragons to sleep, and then drove them from the land, so that they have never been seen there since.

y: From Proto-West Germanic *ansu, from Proto-Germanic *ansuz (“god, deity”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ems- (“engender, beget”). Cognate with Old Norse áss.

s: alternative sense for the runic character ᚩ (/o(ː)/)
ᚩ (os) byþ ordfruma ǣlcre sprǣċe, wīsdōmes wraþu and witena frōfur and eorla gehwām ēasnys and tōhiht.
ᚩ (mouth) is is the source of every language, Wisdom's support and consolation for the wise; Happiness and hope for every earl.
y: Potentially from a Proto-West Germanic *ōs, Proto-Germanic *ōsaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃éh₁os (“mouth”), or from Latin ōs (“the mouth”). Only found in the Old English rune poem, which is analog to Old Norse runology, where the rune ᚬ (/o(ː)/) later on had the cognate name óss, Middle Norwegian ōs, Old Swedish ōs (“inlet”).
From Proto-West Germanic *Ansuberht, from *ansu (“god”) + *berht (“bright”). Equivalent to ōs + beorht. Cognate with Old High German Ansbert.
From ōs (“god”) + beorn (“warrior”). Cognate with Old Norse Ásbjǫrn.

s:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
⁊ þā wearð ēac ādræfed · dēormōd hǣleð,
Ōslāc of earde, · ofer ȳða ġewealc
ofer ganotes bæð · gamolfeax hæleð,
wīs ⁊ word snotor · ofer wætera ġeþring
ofer hwæles eðel · hāma berēafod.
And then in like manner was Oslac, a beloved man,
a gray-haired man, wise and learned,
deprived of his home, driven out from his homeland,
over the churning of the waves, over the gannet's bath,
over the tumult of the waters, over the whale's homeland.
y: From ōs (“god”) and lāc (“gift, offering”). Cognate with Norwegian Aslak.
From Proto-Germanic *Ansulaibaz, equivalent to ōs (“god, deity”) + lāf (“remnant”).

s: Sēo wīflīċe ōsle ġetimbreþ nest þrēowa on ġēare.
The female blackbird builds a nest three times a year.
Ossett (a market town in West Yorkshire, England).
y: Equivalent to a personal name *Ōsla or ōsle (“blackbird”) + set (“seat”). Attested in the 1086 Domesday Book.

s:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
An. DCCCXXXIII Hēr ġefeaht Eċġbriht cing wið XXXV sċiphlæsta æt Carrum ⁊ þǣr wearð myċel wæl ġesleġen, ⁊ þā Denisċan ahton wælstōwe ġeweald. ⁊ Hereferð ⁊ Wiġþeġn, tweġen bisċeopas, forðferdan, ⁊ Duda ⁊ Ōsmōd, tweġen ealdormenn, forðferdon.

Year 833 In this year King Edgebright fought against thirty-five shiploads of men at Charmouth, and many were slain, and the Danes took control of the battlefield. And two bishops, Herefrith and Wigthegn, and two aldermen, Duda and Osmod, died.
y: From ōs (“god”) and mōd (“mind, heart, spirit”).

s: one of several Anglo-Saxon kings by this name

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
An. DCCXXXI Hēr wæs Ōsrīc ofsleġen, Norðanhymbra cyning, ⁊ feng Ċēolwulf to þām rīċe ⁊ heold VIII ġēr. ⁊ sē Ċēolwulf wæs Cūþing, Cūþa Cūðwining, Cūðwine Lēodwalding, Lēodwald Eċġwalding, Eċġwald Ealdhelming, Ealdhelm Ocing, Ocea Iding, Ida Eopping. ⁊ Brihtwald arċebisċeop ġefōr ⁊ and þȳ ilcan ġēare wæs Tatwine ġehālgod tō arċebisċeope.
Year 731 In this year Osric, king of the Northumbrians, was slain, and Ceolwulf ascended to the throne and held it for eight years. Ceolwulf was son of Cutha, Cutha son of Cuthwine, Cuthwine son of Leodwald, Leodwald son of Edgewald, Edgewald son of Ealdhelm, Ealdhelm son of Ocea, Ocea son of Ida, [and] Ida son of Eoppa. And in the same year Archbishop Brightwald died and Tatwine was ordained as archbishop.
y: By surface analysis, ōs (“god”) + rīc (“kingdom, empire, dominion”)

s:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
Ōsrēd, þe wæs Norþanhymbra cining, æfter wræcsīþe hām cumenum ġelǣht wæs ⁊ ofslagen on XVIII Kƚ Octoƀ ⁊ his līc liġþ æt Tīnamūþe. ⁊ Æþelrēd cining feng tō nīwan wīfe, sēo wæs Ælflēd ġehāten, on III Kƚ Octobr̃.

Osred, who was king of Northumbria, was apprehended and slain on the 17th of October after coming home from his foreign travels, and his body lies at Tynemouth. And King Aethelred took a new wife, whose name was Aelfled, on the third of October.

y: By surface analysis, ōs (“god”) + waru (“care, protection”).

s:

Syxta wæs Ōswald, Norðanhymbra cyning sē betsta ⁊ sē crīstenesta, sē þissum ilcum ġemǣrum rīċe hæfde.
Sixth was Oswald, the best and most Christian king of the Northumbrians, who ruled over this same territory.
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *Ansuwald, from Proto-Germanic *Ansuwaldaz, equivalent to ōs (“god, deity”) + weald (“power”). Cognate with Old Norse Ásvaldr.

At this time the most noble English kings, Osweo of Northumbria and Ecgberht of Kent, held a discussion and conference between them about what was to be done about the state of the English church.

y: From Proto-Germanic *Ansuwiniz. Equivalent to ōs (“(pagan) god”) + wine (“friend”). Cognate with Old Norse Ásviðr.
From Proto-Germanic *Ansuwulfaz, equivalent to ōs (“god”) + wulf (“wolf”). Cognate with Old Norse Ásólfr.
From Proto-West Germanic *Ansuþrūþi, from Proto-Germanic *Ansuþrūþiz, from *ansuz (“god”) + *þrūþiz (“strength”). Equivalent to ōs + þrȳþ. Cognate with Old Norse Ásþrúðr (whence Icelandic Ásþrúður).
From Proto-Germanic *utraz (“otter”), from Proto-Indo-European *udrós (“water animal, otter”).

Eallum cristenum mannum is beboden þæt hīe ealne heora līchaman seofon sīðum ġebletsian mid Cristes rōde tācne: ǣrest on ǣrne morgen, ōðre sīðe on underntīd, þriddan sīðe on midne dæġ, fēorðan sīðe on nōntīd, fīftan sīðe on ǣfen, sixtan sīðe on niht ǣr hē reste, seofoþan sīðe on ūhtan.

All Christians are commanded to bless their entire body seven times with the sign of the cross: first early in the morning, the second time at nine o'clock, the third time at noon, the fourth time at three, the fifth time in the evening, the sixth time at night before one goes to sleep, the seventh time before dawn.
